questions.question: A sound wave has a period of 0.002 seconds. What is its frequency?
questions.explanation: Frequency = 1 / Period. f = 1 / 0.002 = 500 Hz. The period is the time for one complete cycle; frequency is how many cycles occur per second.

questions.question: A4 is 440 Hz. Which frequency represents A5 (one octave above A4)?
questions.explanation: Each octave up doubles the frequency. A5 = 440 × 2 = 880 Hz. A3 would be 220 Hz (halving), and A6 would be 1760 Hz (two octaves above A4).

questions.question: A recording system uses a 16-bit bit depth. What is the approximate dynamic range?
questions.explanation: Dynamic range ≈ bit depth × 6 dB. For 16-bit: 16 × 6 = 96 dB. This is why CD-quality audio (16-bit) offers approximately 96 dB of dynamic range.

questions.question: A sample rate of 44,100 Hz is used. What is the maximum frequency that can be accurately recorded according to the Nyquist theorem?
questions.explanation: The Nyquist theorem states that the maximum recordable frequency is half the sample rate. 44,100 / 2 = 22,050 Hz: just above the typical upper limit of human hearing (20,000 Hz).

questions.question: A sound source is 2 metres from a microphone. The microphone is moved to 4 metres. Assuming the inverse square law, how does the sound level change?
questions.explanation: The inverse square law states that doubling the distance from a point source reduces the sound level by 6 dB. Moving from 2m to 4m doubles the distance, so the level drops by 6 dB.

questions.question: A track is set to 120 BPM. A producer wants to set a delay time to exactly one beat. What is the correct delay time?
questions.explanation: Delay time (ms) = 60,000 / BPM. At 120 BPM: 60,000 / 120 = 500 ms. This ensures the delay repeats in sync with the tempo, creating a rhythmic echo.

questions.question: A sine wave has a frequency of 250 Hz. Calculate its period in milliseconds.
questions.explanation: Period (T) = 1 / f = 1 / 250 = 0.004 seconds. Converting to milliseconds: 0.004 × 1000 = 4 ms. Period and frequency are reciprocals: as frequency increases, period decreases proportionally.

questions.question: Calculate the file size in megabytes (MB) of a 3-minute stereo audio file recorded at 44,100 Hz with a 16-bit bit depth. Give your answer to the nearest whole number.
questions.explanation: File size (bytes) = sample rate × bit depth × channels × seconds / 8. = 44,100 × 16 × 2 × 180 / 8 = 31,752,000 bytes ≈ 30.3 MB. Dividing bit depth by 8 converts bits to bytes; stereo = 2 channels; 3 minutes = 180 seconds.

questions.question: A track is at 90 BPM. Calculate the delay time in milliseconds for a dotted quaver (⅜ of a beat).
questions.explanation: First, find one beat: 60,000 / 90 = 666.67 ms. A dotted quaver = ¾ of a crotchet beat = 666.67 × ¾ = 500 ms. Wait: a dotted quaver is 3/8 of a beat: 666.67 × (3/8) = 250 ms. This is a classic rhythmic delay value used in production to create a syncopated feel.

questions.question: Explain the relationship between frequency and period. Include the formula and describe what happens to the period when frequency doubles.
questions.sampleAnswer: Frequency and period are reciprocals of each other, described by the formula f = 1/T (or T = 1/f), where f is frequency in Hz and T is period in seconds. When frequency doubles, the period halves: the wave completes twice as many cycles per second, so each individual cycle takes half as long.
keyPoints: f = 1/T and T = 1/f (reciprocal relationship)
Frequency measured in Hz (cycles per second)
Period measured in seconds (time for one complete cycle)
Doubling frequency halves the period
questions.explanation: This relationship underpins all of audio: every pitch we hear is a frequency, and understanding period helps explain phenomena like phase relationships and delay times.

questions.question: Describe the relationship between bit depth and dynamic range. Why does increasing bit depth improve the quality of a recording?
questions.sampleAnswer: Dynamic range in decibels is approximately equal to the bit depth multiplied by 6. For example, 16-bit audio gives roughly 96 dB of dynamic range, while 24-bit gives approximately 144 dB. A greater bit depth means more discrete amplitude levels are available to represent the audio signal. This reduces quantisation noise (the error introduced when rounding continuous amplitude values to the nearest available level), allowing both very loud and very quiet sounds to be captured accurately within the same recording.
keyPoints: Dynamic range (dB) ≈ bit depth × 6
More bits = more amplitude levels available
Greater dynamic range captures louder and quieter sounds accurately
Increasing bit depth reduces quantisation noise/error
questions.explanation: Bit depth directly controls the amplitude resolution of a digital recording. Each additional bit doubles the number of available amplitude levels and adds approximately 6 dB of dynamic range.

questions.question: A recording engineer wants to capture audio containing frequencies up to 20 kHz. Using the Nyquist theorem, explain why a sample rate of 44,100 Hz is sufficient, and what would happen if a 30 kHz frequency were present in the signal.
questions.sampleAnswer: The Nyquist theorem states that the maximum frequency a digital system can accurately represent is half the sample rate. At 44,100 Hz, the Nyquist frequency is 22,050 Hz, which is above the 20 kHz upper limit of human hearing: so all audible frequencies are captured. If a 30 kHz frequency were present, it would exceed the Nyquist frequency and cause aliasing: the signal would fold back into the audible range as a false lower frequency, introducing distortion. Anti-aliasing filters are used before analogue-to-digital conversion to remove frequencies above the Nyquist limit.
keyPoints: Nyquist frequency = sample rate / 2
44,100 / 2 = 22,050 Hz: above the 20 kHz hearing limit
Frequencies above the Nyquist frequency cause aliasing
Aliasing produces false frequencies (artefacts) in the audible range
Anti-aliasing filters prevent this by removing high frequencies before conversion
questions.explanation: The Nyquist theorem is the mathematical foundation for choosing sample rates. 44.1 kHz became the CD standard precisely because it captures the full audible range with a small safety margin, while keeping file sizes manageable.

questions.question: Two identical, uncorrelated sound sources each produce 80 dB SPL. When both play simultaneously, the combined level is approximately:
questions.explanation: Doubling the number of uncorrelated sound sources adds approximately 3 dB (technically +3.01 dB). This is because decibels are logarithmic: combining two equal-power sources doubles the total power, and 10 × log₁₀(2) ≈ 3. So 80 + 3 = 83 dB SPL. You cannot simply add dB values arithmetically: 80 + 80 does not equal 160.

questions.question: A sound wave at 686 Hz travels through air at 343 m/s. What is its wavelength?
questions.explanation: Wavelength = speed ÷ frequency = 343 ÷ 686 = 0.5 m. This formula (λ = v/f) is fundamental in acoustics. Knowing wavelengths helps explain diffraction (sound bending around objects), room modes, and why bass frequencies require larger absorbers to control.

questions.question: What is the key distinction between dB SPL and dBFS?
options: dB SPL measures acoustic pressure relative to the threshold of hearing; dBFS measures digital signal level relative to the maximum value before clipping
dB SPL is used for digital signals; dBFS is used for analogue signals
dB SPL has no reference point; dBFS is referenced to 1 pascal
dB SPL and dBFS are identical measurements expressed in different units
questions.explanation: dB SPL (Sound Pressure Level) is an acoustic measurement referenced to 20 micropascals: the approximate threshold of human hearing. dBFS (decibels relative to Full Scale) is a digital measurement where 0 dBFS is the maximum level the system can represent before clipping. In dBFS, all normal signal levels are negative values (e.g., −18 dBFS). These are fundamentally different scales measuring different things.

questions.question: The frequency ratio for a perfect fifth interval is 3:2. If the lower note is 220 Hz (A3), what is the frequency of the note a perfect fifth above?
questions.explanation: A perfect fifth has a frequency ratio of 3:2. Multiply the lower frequency by 3/2: 220 × 1.5 = 330 Hz. This corresponds to E4 in just intonation. Frequency ratios define musical intervals: an octave is 2:1, a perfect fourth is 4:3, and a major third is 5:4. These ratios explain why certain intervals sound consonant: their waveforms align at regular intervals.

questions.question: Calculate the uncompressed bit rate (data rate) in kilobits per second (kbps) for a mono audio stream at 48,000 Hz sample rate and 24-bit bit depth.
questions.explanation: Bit rate = sample rate × bit depth × channels. For mono: 48,000 × 24 × 1 = 1,152,000 bits per second = 1,152 kbps. For stereo, double this to 2,304 kbps. Understanding data rates helps explain why lossless formats produce larger files than lossy codecs like MP3 (which typically compress to 128–320 kbps).

questions.question: A speaker is measured at 90 dB SPL at 1 metre. Using the inverse square law, what is the approximate level at 4 metres from the speaker?
questions.explanation: The inverse square law states that every doubling of distance reduces level by 6 dB. From 1m to 2m is one doubling (−6 dB = 84 dB). From 2m to 4m is a second doubling (−6 dB = 78 dB). So the level at 4m is 90 − 12 = 78 dB SPL. This applies to point sources in free-field conditions. In real rooms, reflections mean the drop-off is less than the inverse square law predicts at greater distances.

questions.question: Explain how to calculate the wavelength of a sound wave, and describe why low-frequency sounds have longer wavelengths. Include the formula and a worked example using a 100 Hz tone (speed of sound = 343 m/s).
questions.sampleAnswer: Wavelength is calculated using the formula λ = v / f, where λ is wavelength in metres, v is the speed of sound (343 m/s in air at room temperature), and f is frequency in Hz. For a 100 Hz tone: λ = 343 / 100 = 3.43 metres. Low-frequency sounds have longer wavelengths because the speed of sound is constant in a given medium. If fewer cycles occur per second (lower frequency), each cycle must occupy a greater distance to maintain that speed. This is why bass frequencies diffract around obstacles more easily and require physically larger absorbers to control in studio acoustics.
keyPoints: λ = v / f (wavelength = speed of sound ÷ frequency)
speed of sound is constant, so lower frequency = longer wavelength
long wavelengths diffract around obstacles more easily
bass trapping requires physically large absorbers because of long wavelengths
questions.explanation: Wavelength calculations are essential for understanding room acoustics, microphone placement, and acoustic treatment. A 50 Hz bass note has a wavelength of about 6.86 m. This explains why bass traps need to be large and deep (typically a quarter-wavelength thick for effective absorption). Higher frequencies with shorter wavelengths are absorbed by thinner materials, which is why acoustic foam treats mids and highs but not bass.

questions.question: A student claims that combining ten identical loudspeakers playing the same signal will produce a sound level ten times louder than one speaker. Explain why this is incorrect, using decibel calculations to show the actual increase in level.
questions.sampleAnswer: The student is confusing a linear multiplication of power with perceived loudness. Combining ten identical uncorrelated sources adds their acoustic power, giving a factor of 10. In decibels: increase = 10 × log₁₀(10) = 10 dB. However, perceived loudness roughly doubles for every 10 dB increase, so ten speakers would sound approximately twice as loud as one, not ten times louder. The logarithmic nature of decibels and of human hearing means that large increases in physical power produce modest increases in perceived loudness.
keyPoints: combining 10 equal sources = 10× the power
10 × log₁₀(10) = 10 dB increase
perceived loudness approximately doubles every 10 dB
10 speakers sound roughly twice as loud, not 10 times
decibels are logarithmic, matching human perception
questions.explanation: This question tests understanding of the logarithmic relationship between physical sound intensity and perceived loudness. The decibel scale exists precisely because human hearing is logarithmic: we perceive equal ratios of intensity as equal steps of loudness. A 10 dB increase (10× power) sounds about twice as loud. A 20 dB increase (100× power) sounds about four times as loud. This is why adding more speakers in a PA system gives diminishing returns in perceived volume.
